item.title: Thoughts About Identity Loss for Divorced Women
item.description:
Identity

Thoughts About Identity Loss for Divorced Women

Reclaiming self-worth and meaning after the end of a marriage.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Divorced women may lose more than their partner; they can also lose their identity.
  • The identity of "wife" is assumed to be more valuable than the identity of "ex-wife."
  • You don't need to accept that being divorced is "less than" being married.

When you were a married woman, you may have felt safe and secure and things in your life were predictable. The loss of your husband is so much more than just the end of a relationship. It may feel like it strips you of meaning, and many women feel lost. Who am I now?

Sabrina, a woman in one of my groups, remarked: “I keep saying ‘we.’ We saw that movie. We love that restaurant. We had a great vacation in Punta Cana.” She said she’s struggling with the language and language matters. It would sound weird to say: “I had a great vacation in Punta Cana.” It sounds like she went by herself.

Her operating system is still running on “wife.” She went on to say, “While I don’t consider myself a wife anymore, much of my identity and behavior is woven into being that person.” After 27 years of marriage, she doesn’t know who she is without it.

She said she chokes on saying, “my ex.” Ex-husband conveys what society assumes it means. That you grew apart and worked on it but couldn’t solve the problems. Not at all the reality of a woman who has been abandoned. Plus, she used to be the one people came to for support, the one others could rely on. Now she hates appearing like a hero because she’s surviving as a struggling single mom who needs other people’s help. She has an identity, but it’s not the identity she wants.

The Challenge of Moving Forward After Divorce

You’re at a crossroads. You can’t go back; that’s not an option. But it may feel like if you move on, you are accepting all the hurt that was thrown your way. After all, isn’t moving on exactly what your former husband wants you to do? It may feel that moving on would be not honoring the pain. Maybe part of you doesn’t want to give it up. As long as you are suffering, the world can see what he did to you and shake their proverbial heads saying, “Do you believe what a low-life he is?!?”

You are transitioning from an identity that you cherished, being a wife, to one that you may feel is cloaked in shame, being an ex-wife. But thinking that being an ex-wife is shameful or “less than” is a belief, not a fact. What about if you started to shift your thinking so that you could erase that self-limiting belief and start to neutralize it? If roughly 40% of marriages in the U.S. end in divorce, that means that you are part of a large number of women who define themselves as ex-wife. Can you start re-wiring your thinking so that you can begin to get comfortable in this club you never wanted to join?

It seems to me that two factors are taking place simultaneously. First, there are all the losses that you legitimately need to grieve. The loss of the partner, perhaps the home, financial losses, worries about your children, and the loss of the dream of the future. Those are significant enough.

Source: Krakenimages/Shutterstock

Preserving Self-Worth and Embracing Self-Compassion After Divorce

But do you really need to lose your self-image as a person who is valuable and whose life has meaning, too? Wouldn’t it make it a bit easier if you held your head up high and said to yourself, “I may not have been the perfect wife but he wasn’t the perfect husband either. I tried my best and devoted myself to my marriage. I am deciding to not blame myself for the fact that it ended.”

In other words, to shower yourself with self-compassion as you work through this painful period in your life. When you’re soaked in regret and sorrow, Dr. Kristin Neff, the psychologist who works on self-compassion, would recommend you tell yourself these three things:

  1. "This is a moment of suffering." (This is mindfulness—acknowledging the pain.)
  2. "Suffering is a part of life." (This is common humanity—remembering you aren't alone.)
  3. "May I be kind to myself in this moment." (This is self-compassion—offering yourself grace.)

And then she’d probably recommend that you put your arms around yourself and give yourself a big long hug. You deserve it.

A divorce is the death of a dream. Kristin Neff would remind you that you cannot heal a broken heart by beating it up. Fierce love for yourself and gentle acceptance are the only ways forward, and over time, you will stumble across your new identity that you can learn to cherish, just as you are.

item.title: Is the Documentary "You Can See Everything" Inaccurate?
item.description:
Denial

Is the Documentary "You Can See Everything" Inaccurate?

How "You Can See Everything" blurs meaning and misunderstanding.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • The film "You Can See Everything" blurs fact and ambiguity, avoiding conventional documentary truth claims.
  • Fielder uses language debates to reveal Holmes’ elusive communication style, not miscommunication.
  • "You Can See Everything" explores Holmes’ inaccessible inner world without promising answers.

Note: This post may contain spoilers.

The A24 (meta-) documentary You Can See Everything about Elizabeth Holmes, founder of the now-defunct health technology company Theranos, got the internet abuzz. If you watch it, you will see why. The feature is both thought-provoking and unusual, and the main subjects featured in it—Holmes and her partner Billy Evans—have the screen presence of highly-paid actors playing Holmes and Evans.

As one might expect amid so much attention, there are criticisms as well. A key objection made is that the film is inaccurate. One can see why some people think that. There is, for instance, a scene in the film in which Holmes and one of the directors, Nathan Fielder, debate the meaning of the word “can” in the expression “can run every test.” Holmes insists that the device she is showing to Fielder “can run every test.” Fielder suggests that Holmes is not using the word “can” in the usual way. (Note: In one sense of “can,” I can defeat the world chess champion at chess, namely, it is not physically impossible for me to move the pieces on the board so as to score a victory. But if I say I can defeat the world chess champion, you will take me to be saying something different and altogether false. It may also be that Holmes’ device can run every test in some such sense. That, of course, is not the sense that would have interested either customers or investors.) In another scene, Holmes is shown Abbott and Costello’s “Who’s on First?” comedy sketch, and she seems to either not get or pretend not to get the joke, which involves understanding that “Who,” “What," and “I Don’t Know” are names of baseball players.

These and other scenes may leave viewers with the impression that Holmes simply doesn’t use words in the way most people do, and that perhaps, she is not so much a fraudster as a highly idiosyncratic language user with less-than-stellar communication skills.

Were that the message, the film would be, indeed, inaccurate. Holmes is not in prison because of miscommunication. She falsified financial records, diluted people’s blood with water and had the samples analyzed by real labs then claimed to have used the Theranos device, and she did other similar things.

What Does It Mean for a Film to be Misleading?

However, I am not inclined to view the film as misleading, because I don’t know what, if anything, it is asserting. A conventional documentary asserts—i.e., invites audiences to believe—various claims about the characters and events it depicts, and if the claims asserted are false, the documentary is, to that extent, inaccurate. But You Can See Everything is not a conventional documentary. For one thing, Fielder mentions at the very beginning that he is not “good at science things” and asks Holmes whether that was why she invited him and not someone else better equipped to ask questions about the technology. This can be taken as a disclaimer on his part: Viewer beware.

No less importantly, Fielder and Oppenheim could have spoken to other people better-versed in both the science and in the details of the case. This is what one might get in a conventional documentary. Fielder and Oppenheim do not do that either, and the choice seems deliberate. That too may be taken as a signal to the viewer that the filmmakers did not intend to explain “what really happened.”

One can argue, perhaps, that in engaging with Holmes in a discussion about the meaning of “can,” Fielder was deliberately introducing ambiguity to make the story more interesting. But I am not sure that’s true either. An alternative interpretation is this: Fielder wanted to see how far he could get with Holmes if he played on her turf and started from her own premises. Suppose she really did use the word “can” in an atypical way. Shouldn’t she have nonetheless anticipated that this would lead to a misunderstanding? As for the Abbott and Costello sketch, that may have been bait to see what Holmes would say about it. She can be seen laughing while watching it. That suggests she understood what’s funny. What would she say if asked? She denies she understood. The documentary does not assert that her denial is in good faith. An alternative interpretation is that we see Holmes seizing the opportunity and trying to pull the veil over our eyes while falling for Fielder’s trick.

I, for one, am very glad that Fielder and Oppenheim took the approach they took. The actual story has been covered previously, and more than once. The world doesn’t need another run-of-the-mill Holmes documentary, however accurate. What You Can See Everything offers, instead, is an attempt to penetrate what looks like Holmes’ façade. It does not succeed despite the fact that the team has full access for an extended period of time. It is a bit as though the lodgers with their cameras keep knocking on the door even though they are already inside the house. They never get behind the immaterial partition which separates them from the thoughts of their subjects. Just why that is is one of the themes of the film.

Who Manipulates Whom?

In a widely viewed trailer, Holmes is heard saying to Fielder, “I am engaging with you as a human being” and “I am always being real.” It is really the filmmakers who seem to want to engage with Holmes as a human being, but they only get her to reflect their own intentions back at them. Since their main goal was to create an entertaining feature and they succeeded at that, perhaps, we can hand them the victory. But Holmes’ own play remains a mystery, so one could say they succeed on Homes' terms. In the game of manipulation, Holmes and the film-makers draw.

The feature is unconventional—though, importantly, not in a way that’s parasitic on prior conventions, as when an “invisible” artwork seeks to thwart the expectation that artworks in general have some material bearer. The movie feels genuinely original. It surprises viewers without trying to trick them by leading them to expect one thing and giving them another. The work is exploratory, too. It doesn’t promise to deliver anything in particular—least of all, “the truth about Holmes”—but it delivers.

Precisely what it is that it delivers is not easy to say, but that’s part of its point—and its charm.

I would not call the film inaccurate. Of course, it isn’t accurate either. It is something else.

item.title: The Problem With Pain: Suffering and the Myth of Growth
item.description:
Trauma

The Problem With Pain: Suffering and the Myth of Growth

So what if suffering doesn’t make us stronger?

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Pain can threaten our sense of who we are when it disrupts our roles, relationships, and routines.
  • Pressure to stay positive can make people feel worse about already feeling bad.
  • People can cope without post-traumatic growth.

A friend of ours recently totaled their car in an accident. The resulting concussion was worse. Concussions are never fun, but this one lingered.

It’s often said that pain can help us dig deep, find that extra gear, and become stronger, more resourceful people. Maybe. But pain can also lead us into a maze of suffering, with no clear sense of when, or whether, we’ll find our way out.

With some kinds of pain, we have a reasonable sense of what’s wrong and what recovery will look like. It hurts, but we expect it to pass.

Suffering can threaten our very sense of who we are. The distinction goes beyond the severity of the symptoms: it concerns what the experience means for us as people. Physician Eric Cassell described this threat to the person as central to suffering.

When we’re suffering, it can be hard to believe that what we’re experiencing is temporary. It could go on forever. And even if we come out the other side, will we come out intact? We may feel that something essential is being taken from us. We may question our purpose, see ourselves as burdens to loved ones, or feel that we’ve lost the capacity to care for ourselves or contribute to others. Suffering may begin with a physical injury, but its effects reach much further.

That’s what our friend is dealing with. The symptoms, the uncertainty, the disrupted routines, the inability to participate in work and social life as before.

How Should We Support People Who Are Suffering?

So how should we support the people we care about who are suffering?

It’s not always clear. But putting pressure on them to be positive can worsen the burden. On top of what they’re already going through, they may feel added guilt for not handling it better. Research by Brock Bastian and colleagues suggests that feeling pressure not to experience negative emotions can make people feel worse. Post-traumatic growth seems like a big ask when someone is just trying to cope.

There’s also reason to be cautious about the claim that suffering makes us stronger. People sometimes report growth after trauma, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they’ve changed in the ways they believe they have. In a prospective study of undergraduates, Patricia Frazier and colleagues found that reported growth generally did not correspond to changes measured before and after a traumatic event. The story we tell afterward may help us make sense of the experience, but that doesn’t mean it describes a measurable change.

And that’s OK. People can cope without growth. In two studies of people exposed to war or terrorism, Stephen Levine and colleagues found that participants with the greatest resilience reported the least post-traumatic growth. Here, the researchers defined resilience as the absence of post-traumatic stress disorder. People don’t need to emerge stronger to have coped well, and the process of coping may not leave much left in the tank.

Supporting Sufferers with Practical and Emotional Help

Instead of asking them to change their perspective, we can start by taking their symptoms and suffering seriously. Listen without trying to supply a silver lining. Support modest, achievable goals that matter to them, while recognizing that their capacity may change from day to day. Help with practical burdens.

Specific help that addresses a concrete need is often easier for them to accept. Take care of an errand. Bring over a casserole. Keep it simple, too; don’t make your friend have to organize your assistance. And remember: they may be in that maze for a while. That means they may still need help long after the initial attention has faded.

When we offer encouragement, it should be concrete and credible. Acknowledge something they’ve managed or a difficulty they’ve faced. We don’t have to make the situation sound cheerful or promise that everything will work out.

We can care about their recovery without requiring them to find a lesson in it. And we can keep showing up while they find their own way through.

item.title: Building Community Takes More Than an Invitation
item.description:
Relationships

Building Community Takes More Than an Invitation

What a table can teach about belonging, vulnerability, and making connections.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Community develops through repeated acts of attention, participation, and mutual care.
  • Building connections requires vulnerability because invitations cannot guarantee acceptance.
  • New family traditions can create belonging during transitions when they reflect the people involved.

I’ve been reading The Middle of Somewhere: Rural Education Partnerships and Innovation, edited by Hartman and Klein, a book about rural school communities and partnerships. As I read, I keep thinking about the energy it takes to build a community. It involves learning what matters to people, finding ways to contribute, and being willing to receive what others offer. Those ideas stayed with me while watching Hallmark’s Who’s Coming for Christmas? The main character's wish to fill her Christmas table raises a question that extends well beyond the holidays: How do we create a community when we are still trying to find our place in it?

Making Room for Connection

Rhiannon Fish and Jake Foy.
Source: Hallmark Media

Julie just moved to Pine Tree Lane. She is learning a new job as the head librarian, getting to know her neighbors, and imagining what her life might become. After meeting a neighbor, who is a divorced father, and his daughter, a voracious reader who also writes poetry, she explains her dream of having a full table for Christmas.

Two of the dining room table seats were to be held for Julie’s parents, but they won a Christmas cruise. Facing an empty table in a town where she’s starting over, she begins to doubt that she’ll have anyone at her table for Christmas. She must decide to build her community by meeting new people who will fill her table or put aside her dream until next year and dine alone. Mark agrees to introduce her to community members, sold on her optimism about meeting eight people to fill her Christmas table.

Julie’s dining room table represents more than a place to eat. It represents something many of us want when we move or experience a major transition: people with whom to share our lives. We may know where to buy groceries, get a haircut, and how to get to work long before we know whom to invite over or call when we need company. Julie approaches that uncertainty with optimism and vulnerability. She needs to both let people know that she wants to spend time with them and hope that they would like that, too.

The Social Identity Model of Identity Change offers a way to understand what both Julie and Mark are building. This model suggests that maintaining meaningful group connections and developing new ones can help us adjust during life transitions. Julie’s grandmother’s table symbolizes continuity with her family, while her invitations create opportunities to become part of a new community. Mark is maintaining his connection with Vanessa while exploring how their holiday traditions and local relationships can grow following his divorce. Viewed through this lens, both characters are finding ways to carry meaningful parts of their lives into a future that includes new sources of belonging.

Community Takes Give and Take

Julie is also building community through her work at the library, especially among young readers. Books offer a starting point for connection. A shared interest can open a conversation, and returning to a welcoming space can give people opportunities to become familiar with one another.

Mark’s daughter, Vanessa, loves reading and writing. Her interests offer a way for Julie to connect with her as a person with ideas and stories worth hearing. That attention matters. Creating community involves learning who people are and making room for what they bring. In fact, Vanessa is the first to share her poetry at the Christmas Voices event Julie organizes to increase interest at the library.

Building community also involves receiving. We may find it comfortable to offer help, organize an event, or invite someone to dinner. Accepting help can feel more exposing. It means acknowledging that we have needs, sharing those needs with others, and allowing someone else to see those needs and respond. Whether we’re new to a community or building a new community of friends, this can be challenging. For Julie, building community means allowing other people to help shape the life she is creating.

The Vulnerability of an Invitation

Julie begins to believe that her table will be full in time for Christmas and can’t help but feel disappointed as people begin cancelling. An invitation can seem like a simple gesture until we wait for an answer or see those plans unravel. All of a sudden, a simple invitation becomes much bigger than spending an evening together.

For someone establishing new relationships, a cancellation may have us asking uncomfortable questions. Did I misunderstand our connection? Was I too eager? Do I matter to these people? Those feelings can arise even when the cancellation has a reasonable explanation. In Julie’s case, weather disrupts plans. Disappointment is real, but it does not necessarily tell us how much others care.

Nurturing community requires willingness to remain open through this uncertainty. That does not mean repeatedly pursuing people who show no interest. It means leaving room for relationships to develop without asking each interaction to prove that we belong.

Hallmark vs. Psychology

Hallmark: A Christmas table offers a visible, satisfying picture of people coming together.

Psychology: The relationships around that table depend on what happens beyond the celebration: paying attention, following through, accepting help, and reaching out again.

The Verdict: Hallmark is on the right track but misses the full range of community building. A full table is one possible expression of community. A smaller gathering can hold meaningful connection, too.

The book I’m reading has prompted me to think about how much participation community asks of us. Julie and Mark remind me that this includes the willingness to be new, to need people, and to make an invitation without knowing exactly how it will be received.

item.title: Examining a New Challenge for Young Athletes: Free Time
item.description:
Boredom

Examining a New Challenge for Young Athletes: Free Time

Free time: An adult-created problem for youth, and its simple solution.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • Not knowing what to do with free time leads many young athletes/performers into an emotional struggle.
  • Overscheduling by parents, coaches, and instructors has disrupted kids' learning to use their own time.
  • Youth-involved adults need to stop overscheduling young performers and give them time to live their own life.
A teenager struggling with what has become a common challenge for young people, especially athletes who sruggle with what to do with free time and the boredom encountered.
Source: AI-Generated

Sad and bewildering.

A surprising predicament has emerged in recent years for many young people. It’s a difficulty that's become a common experience for athletes, especially for those whose sporting careers have grinded to a halt for various reasons.

Many middle school, high school, and college youth are anxiously perplexed with what to do with all the unstructured free time they now possess since the ending of the overstructured time produced by their organizational athletic involvement. They are bothered to the point of sadness and even depression. It's an issue shared by young people in my office on a daily basis.

They often spend much of that time alone, idly sitting and pondering what to do while endlessly scrolling a screen. Many view such aimless phone or computer time as a waste (true), multiplying their distress. A further bother is the belief that they are supposed to be constantly busy with structured activity. Unbusy time, especially when alone, is experienced as confusing, unproductive, and problematic.

One descriptor frequently crops up when kids share this problem: boredom.

Not that long ago, such extended, unbusy time after school, between classes, during weekends, vacations, and etc. was viewed with an entirely different perspective—freedom. Free to choose whatever you wanted to do without the externally structured demands of parents, teachers, coaches, and other adults. It was joyously anticipated and experienced as “me time,” purposefully spent with one’s own choosing.

What in the world has happened, causing that change in perspective, and what can be done to flip the switch from “boredom” back to a “freedom” experience? Time to explore.

How We Got Here

There’s a wide range of factors contributing to this surprising quandary, including screens, social media, lack of childhood free play, and overstructured time forced on youth by parents, coaches, and other performance instructors. Research identifying those elements is detailed by Jonathon Haidt in his bestselling book, The Anxious Generous (2024). Simple observation reveals the damage of screens to young people with or without scientific study.

We will focus on what parents, coaches, and the current sports/performance culture have contributed to this struggle with unstructured time experienced by young people.

We will begin, briefly, with parents who have denied young children the liberty to be on their own and engage in free play with peers. Kids granted that freedom learned how to independently use time at an early age without the need for adult supervision and structure. Such conditions were commonplace up until the 1990s.

While parental restriction of independent free play is well intended for safety reasons, it disrupts the ability for young people to develop the skill of purposefully using their own time. Other parental overstructure further limits that ability.

Next, we examine the contributions of youth coaches and instructors.

An Overstructured Youth Sports/Performance Culture

Previous Sports Between the Ears pieces You're Far More Than an Athlete | Psychology Today The Hazards of an Athletic Identity | Psychology Today detailed the damaging impact of the overscheduled world of youth sports and other skill-based activities. Today’s focus is on how overstructured extra-curricular activity has disrupted young people’s ability to learn how to use their own time.

Examples of this include coach/instructors, demanding year-round, near-daily participation in a sport, music, theater, or other skill-based activity. Other samplings of such behavior are bodybuilding-obsessed trainers expecting young athletes to work out on a daily basis. Many of these coaches, instructors, and trainers not only insist on this regimented commitment to an activity, but they also force or even threaten participants to do it.

Early over-scheduled engagement with sports, music, theater, or other similar endeavors has resulted in young people being immersed in an adult-structured life with little time to themselves. Some kids are signed up for multiple overlapping activities, running from one to another on the same day with little leftover time to make their own choices. Busy, busy, busy.

When asked how much time they have to themselves during a typical school day, most interviewed middle school and high school-aged students typically say one to three hours. The bulk of that time occurs in the evening at home when and where choices are limited. Most of it is spent on homework, scrolling a screen, or napping. The latter two are understandable given their exhaustion from a busy, non-stop day.

They have minimal opportunity to rest, discover new interests and hobbies, and use their own time with independent choices.

The Solution to a Vexing Problem

Hey, youth-involved adults, please knock it off. Stop overstructuring kids and give them time off to make their own choices and learn to live independently.

Parents, please permit free play and allow kids to choose their own activities. They also can stop signing up kids for multiple, overlapping activities and saying “no” to overzealous coach/instructors and trainers. Let kids play and practice sports on their own. Give sons and daughters a chance to develop interests and skills beyond a sport or other adult-organized activities.

Coaches/instructors and trainers can limit their time expectations for youth participants. No need for year-round, daily practice and training. Give ample time off. Not only will that give kids a chance to learn what to do with unstructured time, it will also prevent overuse injuries, physical and mental exhaustion and burnout resulting from never-ending activity as detailed in this study by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), Overuse Injuries, Overtraining, and Burnout of Young Athletes (Brenner et al, 2024). Improve performance, don't wreck it.

The kids can do something about it as well. They can decide to put the brakes on an unrequired activity. Obviously, they are limited to do that during in-season requirements, but out-of-season practice/rehearsal is a different story. They can also choose to quit a team or other activity if it’s too much.

Their life, their choice.

item.title: Marriage, Fairness and the Myth of Equality
item.description:
Marriage

Marriage, Fairness and the Myth of Equality

Same doesn't mean equal, and equal doesn't mean the same.

Posted November 1, 2026

Key points
  • When you find yourself thinking in terms of fair or not fair, you’re in binary thinking.
  • Dichotomous thinking leads to a one-narrative relationship: one truth (yours), one opinion (your partner’s).
  • You can be in an equitable relationship without everything being equal or fair.
  • Swap “it’s not fair” with “The truth is...” Choose vulnerability over fairness.
Choose vulnerability or fairness.
Source: Galit Romanelli

Co-authored by Galit Romanelli

Alice and Dov decided to open their marriage three years ago.

They’ve been together since high school and never had sex with anyone else. After three kids and 20 years together, they wanted to shake things up. It was Dov’s idea, but Alice also thought it could be interesting.

Pretty fast, Dov had an unsatisfying sexual encounter. His affair wasn’t completely disclosed, and ended abruptly in a major fight.

Alice wanted to have an affair as well, but it didn’t work out for her. The man she was talking to disappeared. The open marriage was getting too messy, so Alice asked that they close up their marriage again.

Dov reluctantly agreed, even though he wasn’t done with his erotic adventures.

I met them a year later in the clinic.

Alice was about to go on an extended work trip, where she might meet the man she previously corresponded with. She said, “Now, it's my turn to have sex with someone else, just like you had.”

She asked to open the marriage one-sidedly.

Dov was supportive at first, as he recognized the historical imbalance.

Alice began texting and sexting her lover.

The more she got into it, the more upset Dov became.

Dov finally said, "It's not fair. It's really not fair. I had one affair. It wasn’t really legit and immediately got shot down. Yours is not only allowed, but also longer and more emotional than mine."

Alice kept giving him examples and reasons why it was fair that now it was her turn.

I finally said to Dov, "Okay, I know that you want this to be fair. Let's talk about it for a moment. I’m going to say something you won’t like: There is no fair in marriage. Marriage is a two-narrative relationship where subjective is the only objective."

"When you say fair, notice for a second. Is that coming from the adult part of you, or from the child part of you?"

He thought for a moment and shyly said his child part.

He wasn't proud about it. But it was stronger than him he said. “In my mind I know it’s her turn, but in my body, this screams injustice!”

Relationships aren't fair.

When you find yourself thinking in terms of fair or not fair, you're in binary thinking. Such split perception usually comes from your childish part. We previously described the three identities in every partner: parent, partner, and child. Your child archetype sees life, and your relationship, as a binary: Either you or me. My turn or your turn. If you’re allowed, then I’m also allowed.

Such binary thinking can be seen as a defense mechanism that once served us. As children we needed to make sense of a complex world fast, while protecting ourselves. That’s why it's natural and unavoidable to think in black-and-white terms sometimes.

In relationships, binaries lead to a lose-lose mentality that keeps couples in shallow intimacy. Dichotomous thinking leads to a one-narrative relationship, with one truth (yours) and one opinion (your partner’s).

Two-narrative relationship

Mature intimacy enables, requires, and emphasizes multiplicity and differentiation. Multiplicity is being connected to multiple parts of myself. Differentiation is my ability to hold both of our truths.

In a two-narrative relationship, we recognize that we’re two different people, with different perceptions, values, priorities and truths. When we’re differentiated, we can more easily access our prefrontal cortex, and fully accept that subjective is the only objective in mature relationships.

Equal ≠ same

Equal means the same amount or the same treatment for both partners, which is impossible in any relationship.

Fair is a judgment about whether something is deserved or just. It’s subjective, because each partner has a different sense of what they deserve. Fair is a problematic concept in two-narrative relationships.

Equitable means adjusted. Partners end up on level footing, even when the needs and skills differ. In the clinic we like to call this meeting at eye level, with responsibility being shared.

“Same doesn't mean equal, and equal doesn't mean the same.”

You can be in an equitable relationship without everything being equal or fair. That's the power of a mature, differentiated relationship.

In our marriage, Galit does most of the cooking. I do all the laundry. Galit leads our social life. I’m in charge of the finances and payments. The load in each of these departments is not equal or “fair.” Each of us holds different levels of responsibility.

Complexify your relationship

If you want a deeper marriage, you will have to move from fair/unfair perception to a more nuanced, subjective consciousness.

When you find yourself thinking in fairness terms, that's a sign a boundary has been crossed. Stop and drop down to your body. Ask yourself what happened? What button got pushed? Where is the perceived “injustice”? Where do you feel unseen, disrespected, or not celebrated enough?

Once you have some clarity, dare to share those insights.

Those insights are your vulnerability.

Sharing the subjective feeling or insight, instead of the objective fair/unfairness, is what will enable you both to hold both narratives.

You can use the prompt “The truth is…”

Dov took a couple of deep breaths and shared, “The truth is… I’m worried you might like him more than me and leave me for him.”

That was his button. She smiled and said that she loves him and he has nothing to be worried about.

They pivoted from fair/unfair, to holding both of their wants.

Swap "it's not fair" with "I don’t feel seen” or “I’m worried you’ll leave me”.

Choose vulnerability over fairness and see how this shift will help you move from a binary, lose-lose dynamic, to a differentiated two-narrative relationship where you can feel free together.

Galit Romanelli is a relationship coach, Ph.D. candidate, and co-creator of The Remarriage Roadmap.
